question: On Friday 1 March 2024, thousands of Greek expats that were registered on the Greek electoral rolls since 2023 received an email from MEP Anna-Michelle Asimakopoulou with the subject line ‘AnnaMichelle Asimakopoulou | 100 days to go to the European elections’.

This was within moments of receiving an informational email sent by the Greek Ministry of the Interior, which is the authority responsible for conducting the European elections in Greece. Ms Asimakopoulou’s email contained text1, photos, a two-minute video clip promoting her political activity, a link to sign up to a newsletter, etc.

In other words, it was a classic example of political advertising in a pre-election period. Indeed it was targeted advertising as it was addressed exclusively to Greek expats who have the right to vote by post. Thousands of recipients have already complained publicly about the fact that they never consented to their data being handed over and processed for the reasons in question.

Indeed, since the Greek Ministry of the Interior is the only body authorised to keep up-to-date lists of voter data and contact details, it is almost certain that the mailing list was leaked to Ms Asimakopoulou from there.

In view of this: What is the Commission's position regarding this blatant personal data leak and the violation of the rights of thousands of citizens through the breach of the GDPR also bearing in mind the extremely sensitive pre-election period?

‘Dear friends, The European elections in Greece are taking place 100 days from now, on 9 June, and thanks to the historic reform enacted by the government of Kyriakos Mitsotakis, you, as Greek expats, will be able to exercise your democratic right by postal vote. The countdown has begun!

Over the next 100 days I will be sending you regular updates on the priorities of the European People's Party and New Democracy, in view of the European elections, as well as on my own actions and my campaign titled ‘Apo Akri se Akri’. Follow me on social media and sign up for my newsletter by clicking on the ‘Sign up’ button. Let’s move forward!’
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2024) As the Commission pointed out in its answers to written questions P-000708/24 and P000815/24, Member States have a primary responsibility to monitor the application of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation — GDPR)1 and to take the necessary steps for enforcement.

Enforcement of the GDPR lies with the EU-27 independent national data protection authorities and courts, who investigate complaints, provide advice on data protection issues and determine when the GDPR has been breached. The Commission understands that the Greek data protection authority investigated this matter and has imposed fines for the violation of several GDPR rules2.
As a general rule, the Commission does not comment on ongoing investigations. The European Data Protection Board is responsible to ensure consistent application of the GDPR.

In the run up to the 2019 European Parliament elections, it issued a statement on the use of personal data in the course of political campaigns3, which complements the Commission guidance on the application of EU data protection law in the electoral context4.

The Commission Recommendation on inclusive and resilient elections 2023/2829, issued as part of the Defence of Democracy package5 on 12 December 2023, acknowledges particular and far-reaching Member States’ responsibilities to foster broad and inclusive democratic participation and to promote free, fair and resilient elections in the EU.

The Commission works closely with all Member States’ competent authorities to promote free and fair elections in the EU and support the exchange of best practices on elections, including in the framework of the European Cooperation Network on Elections6.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection

of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1–88. 2 https://www.dpa.gr/sites/default/files/2024-05/16_2024%20anonym_0.pdf 3 Statement 2/2019 on the use of personal data in the course of political campaigns: https://www.edpb.europa.
